metadata.summary: This evidence-informed expert consensus revises the international terminology used to classify retinopathy of prematurity. It addresses retinal zones, vascular changes, disease stages, aggressive disease, retinal detachment and circumferential extent. It also defines terminology for regression, reactivation and long-term sequelae, including findings after laser or anti-VEGF treatment.

target_population: Premature infants at risk for retinopathy of prematurity
Patients with a history of premature birth

toxicities.event: Exudative stage 4 retinal detachment after laser treatment
recognition: It occurs most commonly within days after laser treatment and is typically convex, sometimes localized, and self-limited.

toxicities.event: Persistent avascular retina after anti-VEGF treatment
recognition: Peripheral retinal vascularization remains incomplete after ROP regression; the avascular area may be peripheral or posterior.
Compared with peripheral persistent avascular retina after spontaneous regression, it appears to occur more frequently and to involve a larger retinal area after anti-VEGF treatment.

Reactivation is more frequent after anti-VEGF treatment than after spontaneous regression. Available evidence suggests that it occurs most commonly between 37 and 60 weeks’ postmenstrual age, although it may arise significantly later, particularly after reinjections.
Findings range from a new, self-limiting demarcation line to reactivated stage 3 with plus disease; the usual sequence of acute ROP stages need not occur.

Recurrent vascular dilation or tortuosity, delicate extraretinal new vessels, hemorrhage around those vessels, or a fibrovascular ridge may be present. Fibrosis, contraction, and tractional detachment can follow.

therapies_index.name: anti-VEGF therapy
therapies_index.administration: Intravitreal injection; no dose or treatment schedule is specified.
key_toxicities: Reactivation occurs more frequently after anti-VEGF treatment than after spontaneous regression; the latest possible time of reactivation is unknown.
Persistent avascular retina after anti-VEGF treatment appears to be more frequent and to involve a larger retinal area than after spontaneous regression.
monitoring: Document the location and extent of persistent avascular retina.
Assess for reactivation, which current evidence suggests occurs most commonly between 37 and 60 weeks’ postmenstrual age but may occur significantly later, particularly after reinjection.

therapies_index.name: laser photocoagulation
key_toxicities: Exudative stage 4 retinal detachment occurs most commonly within days after laser treatment.
monitoring: Document the location and extent of persistent avascular retina if regression is incomplete.

artifacts.title: Table 1. Summary of Key Components of International Classification of Retinopathy of Prematurity, 3rd Edition Classification
artifacts.source_heading: International Classification of Retinopathy of Prematurity, Third Edition

rows: a. Definition of 3 retinal zones centered on the optic disc. The location of the most posterior retinal vascularization or ROP lesion denotes the zone for the eye.
b. Definition of a posterior zone II region that begins at the margin between zone I and zone II and extends into zone II for 2 disc diameters.*

c. The term notch is used to describe an incursion by the ROP lesion of 1e2 clock hours into a more posterior zone. The ROP zone for such eyes should be noted by the most posterior zone of retinal vascularization with the qualifier “notch” (e.g., “zone I secondary to notch”).*

2. Plus and Preplus Disease. Plus disease is defined by the appearance of dilation and tortuosity of retinal vessels, and preplus disease is defined by abnormal vascular dilation, tortuosity insufficient for plus disease, or both. Recognition that retinal vascular changes in ROP represent a continuous spectrum from normal to preplus to plus disease, with sample images demonstrating this range.* These changes should be assessed by vessels within zone I, rather than from only vessels within the field of narrow-angle photographs and rather than from the number of quadrants of abnormality.*

3. Stage of Acute Disease (Stages 1e3). Stage of acute disease is defined by the appearance of a structure at the vasculareavascular juncture as stage 1 (demarcation line), stage 2 (ridge), and stage 3 (extraretinal neovascular proliferation or flat neovascularization). If more than 1 ROP stage is present, the eye is classified by the most severe stage.

4. Aggressive ROP. The term aggressive-posterior ROP was used previously to describe a severe, rapidly progressive form of ROP located in posterior zones I or II. Because of increasing recognition that this may occur beyond the posterior retina and in larger preterm infants, particularly in regions of the world with limited resources, the Committee recommends the new term aggressive ROP.*
a. Stages of retinal detachment are defined as stage 4 (partial: 4A with fovea attached, 4B with fovea detached) and stage 5 (total).

b. Definition of stage 5 subcategories: stage 5A, in which the optic disc is visible by ophthalmoscopy (suggesting open-funnel detachment); stage 5B, in which the optic disc is not visible because of retrolental fibrovascular tissue or closed-funnel detachment; and stage 5C, in which stage 5B is accompanied by anterior segment changes (e.g., marked anterior chamber shallowing, iridocorneolenticular adhesions, corneal opacification), suggesting closed-funnel configuration.* Additional descriptors of funnel configuration (e.g., open-closed) may be applied if clinically useful.
6. Extent of Disease. Defined as 12 sectors in using clock-hour designations.

7. Regression. Definition of ROP regression and its sequelae, whether spontaneous or after laser or antievascular endothelial growth factor treatment. Regression can be complete or incomplete. Location and extent of peripheral avascular retina (PAR) should be documented.*

8. Reactivation. Definition and description of nomenclature representing ROP reactivation after treatment, which may include new ROP lesions and vascular changes. When reactivation of ROP stages occurs, the modifier reactivated (e.g., “reactivated stage 2”) is recommended.*
9. Long-Term Sequelae. Emphasized beyond previous versions of the ICROP, including sequelae such as late retinal detachments, PAR, macular anomalies, retinal vascular changes, and glaucoma.

artifacts.description: An asterisk identifies a change from earlier ICROP publications. The table defines disease extent using 12 sectors, whereas the document’s Extent section specifies 30 sectors; these statements conflict.
artifacts.summary: The table brings together the ICROP3 classification elements for retinal location, vascular abnormality, disease stage, aggressive ROP, extent, regression, reactivation, and long-term sequelae. It also identifies revisions to the earlier classification.
artifacts.clinical_relevance: These definitions support consistent classification and documentation of each eye, including recognition of aggressive disease and changes after treatment.

recommendations.statement: Classify each eye by zone, plus disease, stage, and extent; also record aggressive ROP when present.
recommendations.source_heading: Table 1. Summary of Key Components of International Classification of Retinopathy of Prematurity, 3rd Edition Classification

recommendations.statement: When a notch is present, document the eye according to the most posterior zone reached by retinal vascularization and add the qualifier “secondary to notch.”
recommendations.context: A ROP lesion extends into a more posterior zone than the remainder of the retinopathy.
recommendations.rationale: This distinguishes a localized posterior incursion from disease predominantly located in that posterior zone.

recommendations.statement: Before classifying ROP as zone III, establish that nasal vessels reach the ora serrata and that the 2 nasal-most clock hours contain no ROP.
Assess the spectrum of plus disease using vessels in zone I, rather than relying only on vessels visible in narrow-angle photographs or on a count of affected quadrants.
Continue using the terms preplus and plus while recognizing that vascular abnormalities vary continuously across this spectrum.
When no ROP lesion is visible, the Committee suggests documenting incomplete vascularization together with its zone, rather than describing the eye as having no ROP or an immature retina.
recommendations.context: An incompletely vascularized retina without a ROP lesion.

recommendations.statement: If an eye has more than 1 ROP stage, classify it by the most severe stage present.
recommendations.context: Concurrent stages in the same eye.

recommendations.statement: Use aggressive retinopathy of prematurity (A-ROP) in place of aggressive-posterior ROP.
recommendations.rationale: Its defining features concern progression and vascular appearance rather than posterior location; it can occur farther anteriorly and in larger preterm infants.

recommendations.statement: Use B-scan ultrasonography to determine detachment extent when fibrosis prevents visualization of the posterior pole.

Subcategorize total retinal detachment as stage 5A when the optic disc is visible by ophthalmoscopy, stage 5B when retrolental fibrovascular tissue or a closed-funnel detachment obscures the disc, and stage 5C when stage 5B is accompanied by anterior segment abnormalities.
recommendations.context: Bedside classification of stage 5 retinal detachment.
recommendations.rationale: The subcategories permit classification during bedside examination.

recommendations.statement: Additional funnel-configuration descriptors may be used when clinically useful.
Use regression for disease involution and resolution, and reactivation for the return of acute-phase features.
recommendations.context: Terminology for later phases of ROP.
recommendations.rationale: These processes should not be treated as a simple reversal or repetition of acute ROP.

recommendations.statement: Document the location and extent of persistent avascular retina (PAR).
recommendations.context: Incomplete vascularization following spontaneous or treatment-related regression.
recommendations.rationale: PAR may involve peripheral or posterior retina.

recommendations.statement: Document newly appearing ROP features during reactivation by their presence, location, zone, and stage, using the modifier reactivated for the stage.
If multiple ridges are present during reactivation, apply the modifier reactivated to the more anterior ridge.
recommendations.rationale: The more anterior ridge is typically more active.

recommendations.statement: Classify retinal detachment without signs of active ROP as a sequela rather than attributing it to reactivation.

conditions.name: retinopathy of prematurity (ROP)
conditions.description: A disorder of the developing retinal vasculature in premature infants. ICROP3 classifies each eye by the location of vascularization or disease, vascular changes, the appearance of the lesion at the vascular–avascular junction, and its circumferential extent. It also describes regression, reactivation, and late sequelae.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Findings range from a demarcation line, ridge, or extraretinal neovascularization to partial or total retinal detachment. Posterior vessel dilation and tortuosity range continuously from normal through preplus disease to plus disease. After spontaneous regression or treatment, abnormalities may resolve incompletely, persist, or reactivate.

subtypes.name: preplus disease
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Retinal vascular dilation, tortuosity, or both are abnormal but do not reach the severity of plus disease.

subtypes.name: plus disease
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Posterior retinal vessels show dilation and tortuosity. Iris vascular engorgement, poor pupillary dilation, and peripheral vascular engorgement with vitreous haze can indicate advanced disease but are not required for this designation.

subtypes.name: persistent avascular retina (PAR)
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Vascularization remains incomplete after spontaneous or treatment-associated regression; the avascular area may be peripheral or posterior and is described by location and extent.

subtypes.name: reactivation
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Acute-phase vascular changes or lesions recur after regression. Findings can range from a new, self-limiting demarcation line to stage 3 disease with plus disease and need not follow the usual acute-stage sequence.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess vascularization, vascular abnormalities, lesions, retinal detachment, and visibility of the optic disc.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: During examination and classification of an eye at risk for or affected by ROP.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Record zone, plus disease, stage, and extent for each eye; also note A-ROP if present. A visible optic disc distinguishes stage 5A from stage 5B and stage 5C.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Estimate the temporal limit of zone I during ophthalmoscopy.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: With the nasal edge of the optic disc at one edge of the view, the temporal edge approximately marks the zone I limit.

diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When retinal imaging is used for assessment.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Before 39 weeks’ postmenstrual age, the fovea may be difficult to identify; its position may instead be estimated from the macular center. Plus-disease assessment should not rely solely on vessels visible in narrow-angle photographs.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Show features at the vascular–avascular junction and determine whether a partial detachment involves the fovea.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Particularly when foveal involvement is subtle or difficult to judge clinically.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: An attached fovea corresponds to stage 4A; foveal detachment corresponds to stage 4B.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Determine the extent of retinal detachment.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When fibrosis prevents visualization of the posterior pole.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Can reveal total detachment and its funnel configuration despite an obstructed fundus view.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Characterize vascular abnormalities, avascular retina, leakage, or subtle neovascularization.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When additional vascular assessment is useful, including assessment of late abnormalities or possible reactivation.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: The illustrated findings include persistent avascular retina, leakage in incompletely regressed disease, and leakage at sites of reactivation.
The document illustrates an incompletely developed foveal contour and a poorly defined foveal avascular zone after ROP.

definitions.description: A relatively flat, thin, white demarcation line lies within the retina at the vascular–avascular junction. Peripheral vessel dilation or tortuosity alone does not establish this stage.
A ridge develops from the demarcation line, acquiring width and height. Isolated neovascular tufts called popcorn may lie behind it without constituting stage 3.

Extraretinal neovascular tissue extends toward the vitreous from the ridge. Apparent flat neovascularization in zone I or posterior zone II also qualifies, even without an obvious ridge or demarcation line.
Partial retinal detachment, which may be tractional or exudative.
Partial retinal detachment with the fovea remaining attached.
Partial retinal detachment involving the fovea. A posterior volcano-shaped tractional detachment remains stage 4B if the peripheral retina is attached.
Total retinal detachment with an optic disc visible on ophthalmoscopy, suggesting an open funnel.
Total retinal detachment in which retrolental fibrovascular tissue or a closed funnel obscures the optic disc.
Findings of stage 5B accompanied by anterior segment abnormalities, such as marked anterior chamber shallowing, adhesions, or corneal opacification, suggesting a closed funnel.

staging.additional_rules: The most posterior vascularization or lesion determines the eye’s zone. Zone I extends from the optic disc center to a radius twice the estimated disc-center–to–foveal-center distance. Zone II extends from zone I to the nasal ora serrata, with comparable reach in other directions; posterior zone II extends 2 disc diameters beyond the zone I border. Zone III is the remaining peripheral crescent; its designation requires nasal vessels to reach the ora serrata and no ROP in the 2 nasal-most clock hours. A lesion entering a more posterior zone for 1 to 2 clock hours is classified by that zone with the qualifier “secondary to notch.” When stages coexist, use the most severe stage. Assess the preplus-to-plus spectrum using vessels within zone I rather than a quadrant count or only the narrow-angle photographic field. The document describes extent as 12 clock-hour sectors in Table 1 but as 30 sectors in the Extent section; these statements conflict. Document reactivated lesions with their zone and stage and the modifier “reactivated.”

long_term_effects: Late tractional, rhegmatogenous, or, rarely, exudative retinal detachment.
Retinoschisis that can extend into the macula and threaten visual field or acuity.
Persistent avascular retina, which is prone to thinning, holes, latticelike changes, and later retinal detachment.
Macular abnormalities, including a smaller foveal avascular zone and a blunted or absent foveal depression.
Persistent vessel tortuosity, straightened vascular arcades with macular dragging, a falciform retinal fold, abnormal branching, circumferential vascular connections, and telangiectatic vessels.
Secondary angle-closure glaucoma later in life.
follow_up.survivorship_notes: Describe persistent avascular retina by location and extent. A late detachment without signs of active ROP is a sequela rather than reactivation. Reactivation is reported more often after anti-VEGF treatment than after spontaneous regression and rarely, if ever, after complete laser photocoagulation; current evidence places its most common occurrence after anti-VEGF injection between 37 and 60 weeks’ postmenstrual age, although later reactivation may occur.

conditions.name: aggressive retinopathy of prematurity (A-ROP)
conditions.description: A severe, rapidly progressive ROP phenotype defined chiefly by its pace and vascular appearance rather than by its retinal location. The term replaces aggressive-posterior ROP because this phenotype can occur beyond the posterior retina and in larger preterm infants.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Pathologic neovascularization and severe plus disease develop rapidly without an observed progression through the usual ROP stages. Early findings can include capillary abnormalities, arteriovenous shunting, dilated vascular loops, and extensive loss of vascularized retina. Stage 3 disease may form inconspicuous flat neovascular networks. Posterior disease can produce a volcano-shaped tractional detachment involving the fovea while leaving peripheral retina attached.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify rapid progression, severe plus disease, and neovascular abnormalities.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Flat neovascularization may be difficult to see with a 28-D lens.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Provide greater magnification for assessing subtle flat neovascularization.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When such neovascularization is difficult to visualize during ophthalmoscopy.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Help assess subtle neovascular and vascular abnormalities.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When clinical visualization of suspected flat neovascularization is difficult.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Illustrated A-ROP findings include capillary nonperfusion and vasoobliteration.

staging.additional_rules: Record A-ROP when present. Its progression need not be observed through the usual acute stages; its flat neovascularization is stage 3 disease. A fovea-involving volcano-shaped detachment with attached peripheral retina is stage 4B, not stage 5.

document_sections.heading: International Classification of Retinopathy of Prematurity, Third Edition
document_sections.content: The International Classification of Retinopathy of Prematurity, Third Edition (ICROP3) revises the terminology used to describe retinopathy of prematurity (ROP). The earlier classification appeared in 1984, was extended in 1987 to cover retinal detachment, and was revised in 2005. Reese et al published a classification of retrolental fibroplasia in 1953. The 1984 ICROP was developed by 23 ophthalmologists from 11 countries; its description of acute ROP enabled the Cryotherapy for ROP Study, which showed that ROP could be treated successfully and established the need for screening worldwide for this preventable cause of childhood blindness. ICROP3 addresses subjective elements of classification, advances in ophthalmic imaging, the distinctive regression and reactivation patterns following anti-VEGF therapy, and ROP patterns in regions with limited resources that the preceding system described inadequately. An examination should classify each eye by zone, plus disease, stage, and extent, and should also record A-ROP when present. Table 1 summarizes the retained classification elements and the revisions.

document_sections.heading: Purpose
document_sections.content: This consensus statement establishes standardized ROP classification terminology. A third revision was needed because important classifications can be interpreted differently, imaging has changed, pharmacologic treatments have introduced regression and reactivation patterns unlike those after ablative treatment, and some regional presentations fit the previous classification poorly.

document_sections.heading: Design
document_sections.content: The work combined a review of evidence-based literature with expert consensus opinion.

document_sections.heading: Participants
document_sections.content: The international ROP committee was convened in March 2019. It represented 17 countries and included 14 pediatric ophthalmologists and 20 retinal specialists; 12 members were women and 22 were men.

document_sections.heading: Methods
document_sections.content: The committee first formed 3 groups addressing acute disease, regression or reactivation, and imaging. Those groups identified problems and possible approaches through repeated videoconferences and an online discussion board. The full committee then developed the classification through further videoconferences, 2 multiday meetings in person, and online discussion.

document_sections.heading: Main Outcome Measures
document_sections.content: The intended output was a consensus statement.

document_sections.heading: Results
document_sections.content: ICROP3 retains zone as a measure of location, stage as a description of findings at the vascular–avascular junction, and circumferential extent. Refinements include posterior zone II, notch, subdivisions of stage 5, and recognition that vascular abnormality spans a continuum from normal to plus disease. The term aggressive ROP replaces aggressive-posterior ROP because aggressive disease can affect larger preterm infants and occur outside the posterior retina, particularly in regions with limited resources. The classification also describes regression, reactivation, and long-term sequelae in greater detail.

document_sections.heading: Conclusions
document_sections.content: The classification principles may make ROP care more consistent and improve its quality internationally, while providing a basis for future research and clinical care.

document_sections.heading: Location of Vascularization: Zone
document_sections.content: Retinal vascular growth starts around the thirteenth week of gestation near the optic disc and advances toward the periphery; vascularization is generally complete by approximately term. Its location indicates infant maturity and the risk of developing ROP. Although developing vessels have a lobular distribution and extend nearer the disc nasally than temporally, zones are recorded using circles centered on the disc. Three concentric zones extend toward the ora serrata, and the eye's zone is determined by its most posterior vascularized retinal location or ROP lesion. Zone I lies within a circle whose radius is twice the estimated disc-center–to–foveal-center distance. Zone II extends from the zone I boundary to the nasal ora serrata, with a corresponding distance temporally, superiorly, and inferiorly. Posterior zone II extends 2 disc diameters into zone II from the zone I boundary and identifies disease potentially more concerning than ROP farther out in zone II. Zone III is the remaining peripheral crescent beyond zone II. Assigning zone III requires confirmation that nasal vessels reach the ora serrata and that ROP is absent from the 2 most nasal clock hours. A notch is an extension of a lesion for 1 to 2 clock hours along the horizontal meridian into a more posterior zone than the remaining disease. Record the most posterior zone and qualify it as “secondary to notch”; for example, predominantly zone II disease with a temporal extension into zone I is “zone I secondary to notch,” rather than unqualified zone I disease. With a 28-diopter (D) lens, the temporal zone I boundary can be estimated near the temporal edge of the view when the disc's nasal edge is placed at the opposite edge. Because retinal photographs may not clearly show the fovea before 39 weeks’ postmenstrual age, the macular center may serve as its approximate position. Figure 1 depicts the zone boundaries and clock-hour sectors in both eyes; its illustrative left eye has approximately 3 clock hours of stage 1 disease in zone II.

document_sections.heading: Plus and Preplus Disease
document_sections.content: Severe ROP is associated with posterior retinal vascular dilation and tortuosity, termed plus disease in 1982. The 1984 ICROP selected a representative narrow-angle image, while the Cryotherapy for ROP Study and later trials selected another image to illustrate the minimum dilation and tortuosity required for plus disease. The 2005 revision defined preplus disease as abnormal vascular dilation, tortuosity, or both that falls short of plus disease. Iris vascular engorgement, poor pupil dilation, and peripheral vascular engorgement with vitreous haze appeared in the original description; they are now recognized as signs of advanced disease rather than requirements for diagnosing plus disease. The committee recommends assessing the plus disease spectrum using vessels within zone I, not solely those captured in narrow-angle images or a count of affected quadrants. The terms preplus and plus remain in use, but vascular abnormality is understood as a continuum from normal through preplus to plus disease. Assessments can differ among observers, with better agreement at the normal and severe ends. Clinical severity assessment may also take account of clinical and demographic risks, examination technique, lens power, the zone containing abnormal features, and the rate of progression. Figure 2 illustrates varying combinations of arterial tortuosity and venous dilation in preplus and plus disease; its severe examples include flat stage 3 neovascularization and a presentation typical of A-ROP. For Figure 3, all 34 committee members classified 30 images as normal, preplus, or plus. Their differing judgments about category boundaries, illustrated with 6 representative images and 9 segmented images, support a continuum of vascular severity.

document_sections.heading: Stage of Acute Disease (Stages 1e3)
document_sections.content: A premature infant's retina may not yet be fully vascularized. When there is no ROP lesion, the committee suggests describing incomplete vascularization together with its zone—for example, “incomplete vascularization into zone II”—instead of calling the finding no ROP or an immature retina. Once acute changes appear at the junction of vascularized and avascular retina, stage describes their morphology. If an eye contains more than 1 stage, classify it by the most severe stage. Figure 4 illustrates incomplete vascularization into zone II, with retinal vessels tapering and ending progressively. Figures 5 and 6 illustrate stages 1 through 3 in fundus photographs and OCT images; the OCT examples show how junctional structures correspond between cross-sectional and en face views.

document_sections.heading: Stage 1: Demarcation Line
document_sections.content: Stage 1 has a thin, relatively flat, pale demarcation line within the retinal plane at the vascular–avascular junction. Vessels behind the line may branch abnormally. Dilation and tortuosity confined to peripheral vessels at that junction do not, by themselves, establish stage 1. Figure 5 also illustrates a stage 1 line accompanied by a notch classified as zone I secondary to notch.

document_sections.heading: Stage 2: Ridge
document_sections.content: Stage 2 is marked by a ridge arising from the demarcation line and developing both width and height. Its height varies and its color may range from white to pink. Small isolated neovascular tufts on the retinal surface behind the ridge, called popcorn, can occur but do not amount to stage 3 disease.

document_sections.heading: Stage 3: Extraretinal Neovascular Proliferation
document_sections.content: Stage 3 involves extraretinal neovascular tissue extending from, and continuous with, the back of the ridge into the vitreous. Greater proliferation gives the lesion an irregular outline. In zone I or posterior zone II, extraretinal neovascularization can look flat and occur without a conspicuous ridge or demarcation line; it remains stage 3. The amount of neovascular tissue can vary. Figure 5 includes an eye containing stage 2 and stage 3 findings, associated popcorn, and plus disease. Figure 6 shows extraretinal proliferation both at and posterior to the junction on OCT.

document_sections.heading: Aggressive Retinopathy of Prematurity
document_sections.content: The 2005 ICROP introduced aggressive-posterior ROP for severe, rapidly advancing ROP in zone I or posterior zone II. The phenotype had also been called rush disease and may correspond to florid acute ROP observed in the 1940s. Its original description generally concerned the smallest premature infants. It is now increasingly recognized in larger preterm infants and outside the posterior retina, especially where resources are limited. Because speed of progression and vascular appearance, rather than location, define the phenotype, the committee recommends replacing aggressive-posterior ROP with aggressive retinopathy of prematurity (A-ROP). Its characteristic pattern is rapid pathological neovascularization and severe plus disease without observed progression through the usual stages. Early findings may include capillary abnormalities behind the original vascular border and arteriovenous shunts resembling enlarged loops around vascular injury; in extreme cases, nearly the entire previously vascularized retina may appear lost. Thin zone I vessels can be seen early in more posterior cases. Stage 3 may take the form of inconspicuous flat neovascular networks, which can be hard to see with a 28-D lens; higher magnification, such as a 20-D lens, or fluorescein angiography may help. A-ROP can also show the extraretinal neovascularization typical of classic stage 3. Figure 7 illustrates plus disease, vascular loops and shunts, nonperfusion, vasoobliteration, flat neovascularization, and other appearances of A-ROP; typical staged lesions may be absent.

document_sections.heading: Retinal Detachment (Stages 4 and 5)
document_sections.content: Acute ROP and regression need not have distinct boundaries, particularly when retinal detachment is present: both processes may be seen together. Stage 4 denotes partial detachment and stage 5 denotes total detachment.

document_sections.heading: Stage 4: Partial Retinal Detachment
document_sections.content: Stage 4A is partial detachment with an attached fovea; stage 4B includes foveal detachment. Findings suggesting detachment include diminished fine detail in choroidal vessels or granular retinal pigment epithelium, a ground-glass appearance compared with adjacent attached retina, or both. Macular displacement and straightening of arcade vessels suggest peripheral traction. OCT can be particularly useful for detecting subtle foveal involvement; photographs may not clearly reveal the detachment's extent. Stage 4 can be exudative or tractional, can occur in treated or untreated eyes, and can differ according to traction direction and associated exudation. Exudative stage 4 detachment occurs most often within days after laser treatment and is usually convex, sometimes localized, and self-limited. Tractional detachment accompanies progressive fibrovascular organization and vitreous haze and may coexist with lipid, subretinal hemorrhage, or both. Clinical examination may not readily distinguish retinoschisis from detachment. A-ROP can produce a posterior volcano-shaped tractional detachment, generally involving the fovea while peripheral retina stays attached. Despite resemblance to a funnel-shaped stage 5 detachment, it is stage 4B because detachment is not total. Figures 8 and 9 illustrate stage 4A and stage 4B appearances, including the value of OCT for identifying foveal detachment. Figure 8 includes an example of stage 4A detachment with 360 traction along the peripheral ridge.

document_sections.heading: Stage 5: Total Retinal Detachment
document_sections.content: Stage 5 is total retinal detachment. Funnel configuration has been described as open-open, open-closed, closed-open, or closed-closed according to whether its anterior and posterior ends remain open. If fibrosis hides the posterior pole, B-scan ultrasonography is needed to assess detachment extent. To permit bedside classification, the committee now recommends 3 subdivisions: in stage 5A the optic disc is visible on ophthalmoscopy; in stage 5B it cannot be seen because of retrolental fibrovascular tissue or a closed-funnel detachment; stage 5C combines stage 5B with anterior segment abnormalities, suggesting a closed funnel. Those abnormalities can include anterior displacement of the lens, marked shallowing of the anterior chamber, iridocapsular adhesions, capsule-endothelial adhesion with central corneal opacity, or combinations of these findings. Funnel descriptors such as open-closed may also be added when clinically useful. Figure 10 shows the visible disc and open funnel of stage 5A, the obscured disc and posteriorly closed funnel of stage 5B, and the anterior abnormalities accompanying stage 5C.

document_sections.heading: Extent
document_sections.content: The Extent section states that disease extent is classified in 30 sectors bounded by clock-hour positions. This conflicts with Table 1, which specifies 12 sectors using clock-hour designations; the document does not reconcile the two figures.

document_sections.heading: Regression, Reactivation, and Long-Term Sequelae
document_sections.content: Earlier ROP classifications emphasized acute disease more than regression. Anti-VEGF treatment introduced additional classification challenges because regression and its timing differ from those after laser treatment. For later phases, the committee recommends regression for involution and resolution, and reactivation for the return of acute-phase features. Regression may be complete or incomplete, including persistent abnormalities. Neither regression nor reactivation should be treated as a simple reversal or replay of the acute-stage sequence.

document_sections.heading: Regression
document_sections.content: Spontaneous regression and regression after treatment can have different patterns. The earliest visible signs are generally vascular. They can appear after anti-VEGF therapy as early as 1e3 days, compared with approximately 7e14 days after laser photocoagulation or during spontaneous regression. Plus disease may diminish, but dilation and tortuosity need not improve together: after anti-VEGF injection, dilation may decline before tortuosity, and tortuosity may or may not decline. Vessels may extend into previously avascular peripheral retina spontaneously or following anti-VEGF treatment. Other regression signs include involution of tunica vasculosa lentis, improved pupillary dilation and media clarity, and resolution of intraretinal hemorrhage. Neovascular tissue becomes thinner and whiter as the lesion regresses. Subsequent peripheral vascularization may be complete or incomplete; incomplete vascularization is termed persistent avascular retina (PAR), which may lie in peripheral or posterior retina. Compared with peripheral PAR following spontaneous regression, PAR following anti-VEGF treatment seems more frequent and more extensive. Its location, such as posterior zone II, and extent, such as nasal involvement, should be documented. Figure 11 contrasts regression after laser and anti-VEGF treatment. Its laser example shows a thinner, whiter stage 3 lesion 1 week after treatment and regression at 1 month; anti-VEGF examples show improvement at 2 weeks and 4 weeks, including one eye with more peripheral vascular growth and reactivated stage 1. Figure 12 illustrates PAR and incompletely regressed disease in longer-term examples.

document_sections.heading: Reactivation
document_sections.content: Reactivation is more frequent after anti-VEGF treatment than after spontaneous regression and occurs rarely, if ever, after complete laser photocoagulation. It can follow either incomplete or complete regression of the original lesion. The longest possible interval after anti-VEGF injection is unknown. Current evidence suggests reactivation occurs most often between 37 and 60 weeks’ postmenstrual age, but agent and dose can affect timing, and substantially later recurrence is possible, especially after reinjection. Manifestations range from a new, self-limiting demarcation line to stage 3 with plus disease; progression need not follow the usual acute-stage sequence. Vascular dilation, tortuosity, or both may recur as in acute preplus or plus disease. New extraretinal vessels may be finer and harder to see than in acute ROP, and hemorrhage may surround them. They can instead form a fibrovascular ridge that progresses to fibrosis, contraction, and tractional detachment. Documentation should state the presence and locations of new features using zone and stage with the modifier “reactivated”; a returning demarcation line, for example, is “reactivated stage 1.” Recurrence usually arises at the original ridge, the new leading edge of intraretinal vascular growth, or both, but may also arise elsewhere in vascularized retina. Where several ridges exist, “reactivated” applies to the more anterior, generally more active ridge. Findings may be subtle. Progression to stages 4 and 5 is associated with vitreous condensation or haze, fibrotic contraction, retinal breaks, or combinations of these. Figure 13 illustrates recurrence at different sites and times: reactivated stage 1 is shown at 38 weeks’ postmenstrual age after injection at 32 weeks’ postmenstrual age, and at 68 weeks’ postmenstrual age after injection at 37 weeks’ postmenstrual age. Reactivated stage 3 is shown at 67 weeks’ postmenstrual age after injections at 33 weeks’ and 52 weeks’ postmenstrual age, and at 50 weeks’ postmenstrual age after injection at 36 weeks’ postmenstrual age. Another eye treated at 34 weeks’ postmenstrual age appeared regressed at 38 weeks’ postmenstrual age but had reactivated stage 3 at the original site at 51 weeks’ postmenstrual age without growth into peripheral avascular retina. An image at 100 weeks’ postmenstrual age after injection at 38 weeks’ postmenstrual age shows that residual fibrosis alone does not establish reactivation without increasing vascular activity. Fluorescein angiography at 45 weeks’ postmenstrual age following injection at 34 weeks’ postmenstrual age shows leakage at both the leading edge and original border.

document_sections.heading: Long-Term Sequelae
document_sections.content: People born prematurely may have lasting ocular abnormalities even without a history of ROP. Late detachment may be tractional, rhegmatogenous, or, rarely, exudative. Detachment without signs of active ROP should be classified as a sequela rather than reactivation. Chronic traction from involuted stage 3 can cause retinoschisis that progresses into the macula without detachment and threatens the visual field and acuity. PAR is susceptible to retinal thinning, holes, and lattice-like changes and may be associated with detachment later in life. Macular findings include a smaller foveal avascular zone and a shallow or absent foveal depression; they may relate to acute ROP severity and may be easier to identify with fluorescein angiography or OCT. Vascular sequelae include persistent tortuosity, straightened arcades with macular dragging, falciform retinal folds, abnormal nondichotomous branching, interconnected circumferential arcades, and telangiectatic vessels. Vitreous hemorrhage can occur. Eyes with previous ROP can develop secondary angle-closure glaucoma later in life. Figure 12 includes a combined tractional and exudative detachment in an 18-year-old with untreated ROP, PAR in 7-year-old examples of spontaneously regressed disease, an incompletely regressed ridge and PAR in a 15-year-old followed by macula-involving rhegmatogenous detachment 2 years later, and foveal abnormalities in a 7-year-old previously treated with laser.

document_sections.heading: Conclusions
document_sections.content: Scientific and clinical advances have changed understanding and management of ROP. Since the 2005 classification, developments have included neonatal care, anti-VEGF therapy, ophthalmic imaging, machine learning, and pediatric vitreoretinal surgery. Drawing on literature review and expert consensus, ICROP3 preserves existing measures while refining posterior zone II, notch, stage 5 subdivisions, and the interpretation of vascular abnormality as a continuum without discarding preplus and plus terminology. It replaces aggressive-posterior ROP with A-ROP and establishes terminology for regression and reactivation. The committee expects these principles to support future research and clinical care, while presenting ICROP3 as one step toward better outcomes rather than a final resolution. Further research is needed to quantify vascular change and progression rate, characterize findings with methods such as fluorescein angiography and OCT, clarify long-term PAR risks, and determine the signs and timing of reactivation. Collaboration with other caregivers and investigators may improve the consistency and quality of ROP care worldwide.
